notes: Four developed sections, 40 workbook items and Pensa 10/8/8; full reading and recombination retained, without audio or exceptions. Counts and a repair-money limit determine the transport choice; final selection of five box numbers is still due before Friday.

Five open slots: costare, interrogative quanto (it-quanto-domanda), trasporto, banconota and receptive venerdì. The plan’s it-quanto at 21 belongs to comparison grammar and is not promoted here; the chapter-13 price/quantity question has a separate sense identity. Friday remains productive at planned 15. The two photos stay protected with Elena; Ada’s sealed envelope contains no money in the story and is never opened. The money belongs to the repair budget and is shown by Paolo separately.

The blue-shirt transport worker quotes three hypothetical load prices; he does not claim control of either library. Verbal agreement fixes five boxes plus one shelf at thirty euros, but no payment or loading happens before the exact box numbers are supplied. Friday is tomorrow; the public reading meeting stays tomorrow at three.

Own audit: question-word and quantity-family cards show all displayed forms with accurate mappings; numerical sei retains a separate numeric popup from essere sei. Monetary figures in the prose are spelled out. The high primary-word exposure is supported by counted-object charts and explicit price/quantity consequences; it is not a measured learner-comprehension claim. No transport-payment event is asserted by the prospective full-load calculation; all ten notes remain with Paolo.

Nine delivered SVG aids: one cover, two inline scenes, four vignettes and two diagrams. Counted boxes and symbolic banknotes anchor every numeral at first exposure. The coffee-paying vignette is explicitly a generic example; no transport money has changed hands. Prior coverage is about 80%, below the part-2 advisory 88%; assess the nine numeral labels and other first-use supports together with the full reading, rather than interpreting lexical form coverage as measured comprehension. No waiver is claimed; verify that an absolute beginner can actually infer these words. First-reading dates are preserved and continuity merging is left to finalize.

segments.text: Paolo guarda le scatole blu nella vecchia biblioteca. Le conta con Elena: «Io conto le scatole: uno, due, tre, quattro, cinque, sei, sette». Sono sette scatole blu. Vicino alla porta è una scatola rossa. Paolo guarda la scatola rossa: «Otto». Elena guarda dietro la porta: è anche una seconda scatola rossa. Paolo non guarda dietro la porta e non vede la scatola.

grammar.title: Grammatica
grammar.rule: cinque scatole / sei; venti euro / trenta euro; quanto costa?
grammar.note_en:
Numbers can describe how many things there are or an amount of money. The first table matches each written word with its figure: cinque 5, sei 6, sette 7, otto 8, nove 9, dieci 10, venti 20, trenta 30 and cento 100. Sei can also mean “you are”, as learned earlier; sei scatole means “six boxes”, so the noun and the surrounding sentence identify the number meaning.

Quante scatole? means “How many boxes?”; quanti libri? means “How many books?”; quanta acqua? means “How much water?”; quanto costa? means “How much does it cost?” When accompanying a noun, quanto/quanta/quanti/quante agree with its gender and number. In Quanto costa?, quanto is an invariable question about the amount. Scatole is feminine plural, libri masculine plural and acqua feminine singular. In the price question, quanto asks for the amount. Costa, “costs”, has a singular subject such as il trasporto, “the transport”; costano, “cost”, accompanies plural subjects. A price is an amount requested for a particular service or object; cost is the expense involved in the choice. They overlap in these transport quotes.

The noun euro stays the same in the plural: venti euro and trenta euro mean “twenty euros” and “thirty euros”. A banconota is a banknote; banconote is its ordinary plural. Una banconota da dieci euro means “a ten-euro banknote”; here da identifies its denomination. The volunteers’ hundred euros are ten ten-euro notes. Moving notes into groups lets them compare quotes before making any payment. Pagare means “pay”; counting an amount and agreeing a price do not by themselves mean the money has been paid.

Poco, molto and troppo can describe amounts and numbers. They agree with a noun: poca acqua, “little water”; pochi libri, “few books”; molta colla, “much glue”; molti libri, “many books”; troppe scatole, “too many boxes”. Before a noun, abbastanza means “enough” and does not change: abbastanza euro, “enough euros”. Poco tempo means “little time”. After a verb, quantity words can work as unchanging adverbs: costa poco, “it costs little”; costa molto, “it costs a lot”; costa troppo, “it costs too much”. Enough and too much depend on a purpose or limit: the full transport uses all the repair money, while the smaller load leaves money for glue and wood.

The second table quotes a real choice inside this fictional story: nove scatole e uno scaffale, “nine boxes and one shelving unit”, costs cento euro, “one hundred euros”; cinque scatole, “five boxes”, costs venti euro, “twenty euros”; cinque scatole e uno scaffale, “five boxes and one shelving unit”, costs trenta euro, “thirty euros”. The short rule contrasts cinque scatole / sei, “five boxes / six”, and venti euro / trenta euro, “twenty euros / thirty euros”, then asks quanto costa, “how much does it cost?”.

Venerdì means “Friday”. Here it is tomorrow, and prima di venerdì means “before Friday”: the worker needs the box numbers by the end of today. The date is part of this story, not a rule that Friday always means tomorrow.
